# Research Loop: Build a Small Audit Trail Before Expanding Autonomy

As of: 2026-10-15

For student researchers, the useful starting point for an autonomous research agent is a bounded experiment with inspectable instructions, evaluation rules, records and expenditure. Our interpretation of the supplied sources is that delegation should expand only when repeated tests on unused tasks justify it. Together, these materials support a reviewable pilot; they do not establish a reliable autonomous workflow or promise savings. <!--03-c1 03-c2 03-c4 03-c7-->

## Define what the agent may change

AI Code King’s tutorial illustrates an important boundary: the optimizer changes workflow instructions while the underlying model and grading rules remain fixed. This is instruction optimization, not training model weights. The tutorial also explicitly describes proposed instruction changes as candidates rather than demonstrated results. Its value here is an operational procedure, not evidence of measured improvement. [Tutorial: 00:56, 04:30 and 09:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=56s). <!--03-c1-->

For a student pilot, our recommendation is to make those boundaries explicit before execution: identify the editable instruction file, preserve the starting version and specify the evaluator that will judge both versions. The research question then becomes whether a documented instruction change helps under fixed evaluation conditions. That is a more inspectable question than whether the agent has generally “improved itself.” [Fixed grading rules, 04:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=270s). <!--03-c1-->

Choose the task just as carefully. *Why Try AI* recommends representative work whose outcomes the user can evaluate, fresh chats with equal file and tool access, and judgments supported by specific parts of the answers. We interpret these as useful comparison controls. The author’s preference for ChatGPT in a scoped research example does not establish general superiority; students should carry over the procedure without inheriting the verdict. [Original article](https://www.whytryai.com/p/switch-ai-models). <!--03-c3-->

## Write the record before running the loop

The MIRA preprint describes work orders containing an objective, relevant evidence, resource guidance, acceptance criteria and a stopping condition. It also describes retaining failures and contradictory results in the repository for later decisions. Students can adopt this record structure without assuming that MIRA’s performance transfers to their own projects. [MIRA, Appendix C](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02525). <!--03-c4-->

Our practical inference is to write the work order before launching the agent, then retain the artifacts needed to explain what happened—including unsuccessful attempts. A polished final answer alone would not satisfy this proposed protocol. The record should let a reviewer connect the assigned objective, the attempted change and the acceptance decision, while seeing evidence that challenged the chosen approach. <!--03-c4-->

*Campus Talks* adds a researcher-facing planning perspective: describe study plans before collecting data, share variable descriptions and code, and allow extra planning time. Applied to agent experiments, this supports a prospective review checkpoint: inspect the plan before results influence its framing, and reserve time to review the resulting records. These are methodological recommendations, not controlled evidence that documentation improves agent outcomes. [Podcast: 39:29–39:34, 41:08–41:16 and 54:36–54:40](https://timeshighered.podbean.com/e/campus-talks-how-is-ai-affecting-open-research/). <!--03-c5-->

Budgeting belongs in that checkpoint. AI Code King’s planned experiment totals 48 coding trials before optimizer reasoning, setup or rehearsals. Our inference is that a worker-trial count is an incomplete expenditure estimate: the budget should cover the whole search and its preparation. The supplied evidence offers no basis for promising a cost saving. [Tutorial: 12:31–12:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=751s). <!--03-c2-->

## Expand only when the evidence travels

The next useful evidence is repeated performance on tasks excluded from instruction search. AI Code King proposes fresh sessions, repeated runs and equal limits, and warns that better development results with flat or worse held-out results do not demonstrate transferable improvement. Combining that advice with MIRA’s retained failures and Campus Talks’ code-sharing recommendation, our proposed expansion criterion is repeated held-out improvement accompanied by inspectable code and a complete record of unsuccessful attempts. [Tutorial: 10:53 and 11:35–11:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wMQB33rM28I&t=653s). <!--03-c7-->

The physical-lab contrast reinforces the choice of objective. Periodic Labs’ founders describe full autonomy as a non-goal, prioritizing useful experimental data and tractable bottlenecks. Our interpretation is that students should likewise ask which delegated step serves the experiment. This is a commercially interested practitioner perspective: the same interview describes taking their tools into industry. It supplies neither independent replication nor confirmation of the computational studies. [Latent Space podcast: 50:46–51:39 and 1:15:06–1:16:53](https://www.latent.space/p/periodic). <!--03-c6-->

These evidence roles remain distinct. The tutorials supply procedures without supplied execution logs or measured gains; the podcast offers planning advice; MIRA supplies a record structure whose transfer cannot be assumed. Media transcripts remain provisional, and the deferred ambiguous tutorial passage is excluded here. The defensible student commitment is therefore modest: run a bounded pilot, preserve its failures, account for the whole search and require unused-task evidence before granting broader autonomy. <!--03-c1 03-c2 03-c3 03-c4 03-c5 03-c7-->
